topComments.author: halilBB
topComments.text: The interesting failure here is not phishing, it is that "the email came from the real government domain" was accepted as authorization. A domain proves who sent the message, not that the sender was entitled to ask. Every compliance team I have worked with in payments had the same gap: the legal-request inbox verifies DKIM and the letterhead, then a human decides under time pressure with "law enforcement" in the subject line. What actually works is boring: a published list of the exact channels each authority uses, a callback to a number you looked up yourself rather than one in the email, a required case reference you can verify with the agency, and a hard rule that emergency requests get a minimal data set, never full KYC packages plus transaction history. The part that should worry Revolut customers more than the passport scans is the Bitcoin history: on-chain that data is permanent, so a leaked address-to-identity mapping does not expire.

topComments.text: [Disclaimer: I wrote Rosetta 2, so everything I say is biased by that.] Contemporary out-of-order CPUs are incredibly over-provisioned; microarchitects will justify a new feature by another 0.1% gain on some benchmark. The end result is a CPU that's pretty decent at handling the sort of code bloat that comes from a binary translator. There's also a big tradeoff in adding more optimizations to a binary translator. You would like to be able to precisely handle exceptions (especially ones caused by invalid memory accesses) while presenting a userspace exception handler with an architecturally valid state for the source program. There are some optimizations that would be easy to do in principle but are painful for maintaining this mapping between source program states and translated program states. stories.summary: The `ud2` instruction is an x86 opcode that guarantees an "invalid opcode" exception, used by compilers to mark unreachable code and prevent crashes from unexpected execution. It was named `ud2` because Intel retroactively designated two earlier undefined instruction variants (`0F FF` and `0F B9`) as `ud0` and `ud1` after discovering programs were relying on their undefined behavior, then created `ud2` as the officially supported, architecturally permanent invalid instruction. Unlike its predecessors, `ud2` is a clean two-byte instruction that avoids unpredictable behavior from operand decoding across memory boundaries.

My questions are: How can I defer this function to a worker thread as mentioned in the blog, while keeping the vCPU triggering this request halted but the main event loop running? stackOverflowQuestions.title: Do OpenCL global work dimensions still have to be multiples of the local work dimensions?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: Background In OpenCL, work grids for kernels are specified using overall dimensions, and local (i.e. workgroup) dimensions, a.k.a. overall "sizes" and local "sizes". Unlike in CUDA, where one sets the equivalent of work dimensions and dimensions in terms of workgroups, i.e. two multiplicand dimension sets - the OpenCL formulation allows for overall dimensions which do not correspond to complete workgroups. For example: Suppose you want perform some per-workitem operation on 100 values and you have an OpenCL kernel which expects a workgroup size of 32. In CUDA, you would use workgroup (CUDA "block") dimensions of [32, 1, 1], and grid-of-workgroup dimensions [4, 1, 1], giving you [32*4, 1*1, 1*1] = [128,1,1], and you would have to deal with the slack in the kernel. In OpenCL, at least in principle, you could use workgroup dimensions of [32, 1, 1] and overall dimensions of [100, 1, 1], and the OpenCL driver would take care of kernel threads/work-items running only for global indices 0..99. StackOverflow discussion The OpenCL API reference text for clEnqueueNDRangeKernel (v3.0) discusses constraints on the workgroup and global dimensions, and those do not include divisibility of global work dimensions/work sizes by local work dimensions/sizes. Now, in 2010, this question was asked here on SO: Does Global Work Size Need to be Multiple of Work Group Size in OpenCL? The original answer - from 2010 - said (emphasis mine): ... YES, the global work size must be a multiple of the local work size. " but a later answer, from 2016, says: Before CL2.0, your global work size must be a multiple of local work size, otherwise you will get an error message when you execute clEnqueueNDRangeKernel. But from CL2.0, this is not required anymore . You can use whatever global work size which fits your application dimensions. and this got some upvotes and no comments.
